answer.label: Used by
answer.sourceLine: John McCain demonstrably used this joke and attached Mao’s name to it. The Mao attribution is unsupported; identifying McCain as a documented user does not establish him as its original writer.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: McCain at Harvard’s Institute of Politics, reported December 1999

source.excerpt: It's always darkest before it's totally black.
trail: The Harvard Crimson ↗ records the exact line during McCain’s campaign appearance.
CNN’s transcript ↗ includes both McCain’s use and an anecdote explaining the humorous Mao attribution.

The inspected full Wikiquote entry also points to a 1983 A-Team episode, “The Rabbit Who Ate Las Vegas,” as an earlier television lead. That episode was not inspected, so McCain is identified only as a documented later user, not as the earliest speaker or originator.
source.rightsNote: The joke’s original author and first publication are not established. McCain’s documented modern use is not a public-domain clearance.

author.name: John McCain
author.heading: About John McCain
author.bio: John McCain was an Arizona senator and presidential candidate whose public appearances mixed serious policy arguments with jokes at his own expense. Contemporary reporting and later broadcast footage document his use of this line, but neither establishes that he invented it.

misattribution.truthLine: McCain’s use is documented; the original joke writer is not.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: At the Harvard event, McCain was discussing the financial advantage of George W. Bush’s campaign when he offered this reversal of the familiar darkest-before-dawn proverb. CNN later aired him using the same joke; Bill Kristol recalled McCain explaining that adding Mao’s name made it funnier.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote calls darkest/totally-black a humorous McCain misattribution rather than a sourced Mao quotation.
A December 1999 Harvard Crimson report quotes McCain saying the exact joke and crediting Chairman Mao.
CNN reproduces McCain using the line and Bill Kristol’s recollection that McCain said the Mao credit made it funnier.

schema.claimReviewed: Mao Zedong originated the English joke “It’s always darkest before it’s totally black.”
schema.faqAnswer: Mao Zedong’s authorship is not confirmed. John McCain used the joke with a humorous Mao credit, but its original writer has not been established.
schema.verdictNote: McCain is a documented user, not an established originator.
